transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-28
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Sophie Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Atlas PM), Marcus Nguyen (Atlas Eng), Janelle Carter (Atlas Security)
Links shared: https://redwood.example.com/deck/atlas-demo, https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2.pdf, https://redwood.example.com/console/optimize-suggestions

[00:00] Sophie (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Sophie, I'm the AE supporting Atlas. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya (Atlas): Hi Sophie, Priya here. Marcus and Janelle are on too.
[00:11] Marcus (Atlas): Marcus, yup.
[00:12] Janelle (Atlas): Janelle, hi.
[00:14] Sophie: Awesome. Ethan will run through the demo. We'll keep it practical — show streaming, params, retries and then high-level fallbacks and optimize suggestions.
[00:24] Ethan (Redwood SE): Hi all. Quick agenda: 1) how streaming works and what you see client-side, 2) parameter knobs and tradeoffs, 3) retry/backoff and idempotency patterns, 4) graceful fallbacks and routing, 5) short Q&A + next steps.
[00:40] Priya: Sounds good. We're mainly evaluating for chat inside Atlas Assist—must be sub-300ms p95 for short queries and PHI must not leave our VPC if possible, otherwise strong audit logs.
[00:52] Ethan: Great, thanks. We'll point out hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for latency and data residency as we go.
[01:05] Ethan: Okay starting live: opening the Console, chat gen endpoint. Here you can see a streaming connection — tokens arrive as partial deltas. So rather than waiting for the whole response, you get incremental tokens which is how you meet perceived latency.
[01:22] Sophie: One note: sometimes transcripts show K-V cash instead of KV cache — auto-transcribe quirk, ignore that.
[01:31] Marcus: Can you explain the network path for streaming? We use a Lambda front end -> VPC NAT -> Redwood hosted. If PHI is involved we may need Private.
[01:40] Ethan: Sure. For hosted streaming, TCP + TLS to Redwood endpoints. We support region pinning to reduce RTT. If PHI cannot leave your VPC we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) so bytes never traverse public internet. Dedicated gives you predictability without full private plane.
[01:58] Priya: Latency-wise, what helps more: smaller model or batching?
[02:05] Ethan: Tradeoffs: smaller model reduces per-token latency and cost, but may reduce answer quality. Batching increases throughput and amortizes kernel launch costs — it can increase tail latency for single-shot short queries. For sub-300ms p95 single queries, prefer fewer tokens and smaller MV models; for high throughput, batching helps dramatically.
[02:28] Priya: Understood.
[02:30] Ethan: Now parameters: temperature controls randomness; top_p similar but probabilistic. max_tokens bounds generation length. stop sequences reduce over-generation. Prompt engineering and effective stop tokens save time.
[02:44] Marcus: Do you stream partial tokens per token or per chunk?
[02:47] Ethan: We stream as tokens and small chunks; depends on model and tokenizer. The SDK exposes an event stream with partial text updates; the Console shows the same.
[02:58] [03:00] Sophie: We're showing a sample transcript with a 40-token reply to demonstrate partial update frequency.
[03:08] Ethan: Now retries. If a streaming connection drops mid-response, client should retry with an idempotency key and reconcile partial output. We recommend the pattern: 1) use idempotency key for request, 2) exponential backoff with jitter, 3) if partial tokens were received, re-ask the model to continue from last confirmed token using prefix caching or KV cache if available.
[03:30] Marcus: That prefix caching — do you store prompts on your side? We're concerned about PHI.
[03:36] Ethan: By default we store minimal metadata for caching and you can opt out. In Private deployments, you can keep cache local. Also we have configurable TTLs and redaction hooks. Janelle, happy to run the security docs in a bit.
[03:52] Janelle: Please — send SOC 2 + KMS options. We need HSM support ideally.
[03:57] Sophie: Will do. The link is in the chat (soc2.pdf).
[04:05] [04:15] Ethan: Demoing retries: I simulate a dropped connection. On retry with same idempotency key the server returns either the completed output or a continuation token. For long-running gen, we return a checkpoint token so clients can resume.
[04:30] Priya: What's the recommended backoff schedule?
[04:34] Ethan: Exponential backoff starting at ~300ms, doubling with jitter up to a ceiling (we show 5s in examples). For short interactive flows, keep max backoff lower so UX doesn't stall.
[04:46] [05:00] Sophie: Quick tangent — cost controls. Under Console/Optimize we give token-level cost breakdown, and suggestions like quantized model variants for non-sensitive workloads.
[05:12] Marcus: Tell me more about quantization recommendations. We have GPU constraints and want to minimize cost.
[05:17] Ethan: Optimize will recommend quantization/bitwidth based on your prompt distribution and regen rates. For embeddings or rerank, 4-bit quantized models typically suffice; for chat, we suggest 8-bit on high-quality needs. We can run an analysis during the pilot and share a recommendation.
[05:36] Priya: About graceful fallbacks — if the preferred model is at capacity, what happens?
[05:40] Ethan: Smart routing: requests route by policy. If capacity constrained, Redwood can fall back to a compatible smaller model family, or route to a Dedicated pool. You can configure SLA policies: strict (fail) vs degrade (fallback).
[05:55] Marcus: Is there an observable metric we can use to detect fallback events?
[05:59] Ethan: Yes, Console exposes per-route model used, latency, and a fallback flag. You can alert on fallback counts.
[06:10] [06:30] Priya: Any recommended defaults for temperature/top_p for customer service chat?
[06:34] Ethan: Start with temperature 0.0–0.2 for deterministic responses; top_p around 0.8 if you want some diversity. For knowledge retrieval + grounded responses, lower temperature.
[06:47] Marcus: Can we pin a model version per feature flag?
[06:50] Ethan: Yes, you can pin model versions and do canary rollouts via Console. That ties into rollouts and automatic fallback if the canary fails.
[07:02] Sophie: Walking through a quick curl example: show header for streaming, idempotency-key header, max_tokens.
[07:10] Ethan: (reads sample) curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ...' -H 'Idempotency-Key: <uuid>' — then stream endpoint.
[07:18] Priya: We have a question on billing: token rounding and billing windows?
[07:22] Sophie: Billing meters generated tokens; partial streaming doesn't double-bill. Console shows token breakdown by request and model. For Dedicated we provide committed throughput pricing.
[07:36] [08:00] Ethan: Now a short live smoke test: I'll send a quick prompt 'Summarize this patient note in one sentence' with placeholders to avoid PHI. Streaming shows a token every ~40ms here; you can see the UI update.
[08:28] (demo runs)
[08:38] Marcus: That felt snappy. What's the p95 you see for these short prompts on hosted?
[08:41] Ethan: Depends on model and region; for our medium family in us-west our p95 for 20-token replies is ~220ms in stable tests; but YMMV with network and tokenization. We'll run tests with your infra.
[08:56] Priya: If we need sub-100ms p95, what path?
[09:00] Ethan: Likely Private on-prem co-located or Dedicated with specialized GPUs and aggressive batching settings, plus smaller models and region proximity. We'll scope during pilot.
[09:12] [09:30] Sophie: Quick Q on error modes: timeouts vs server errors vs rate limit.
[09:33] Ethan: For client timeouts, retry with idempotency. For 5xx, retry with increasing backoff. For rate limits, honor Retry-After header. We recommend client-side concurrency limits and a local queue for bursts.
[09:50] Marcus: Any SDKs that handle streaming + reconnection pattern?
[09:53] Ethan: Our SDKs include helpers for streaming and reconnection; examples in GitHub and Console. We'll attach sample client code.
[10:02] [10:30] Janelle: Regarding keys and encryption, do you support customer-managed keys?
[10:36] Sophie: Yes — KMS/HSM support for Dedicated and Private; hosted supports CMK options with audit logs. We'll send the detailed options.
[10:45] Janelle: We need audit log retention options.
[10:47] Ethan: Console supports configurable retention and per-token trace hooks. For PHI you can opt out of content storage entirely and only store minimal telemetry.
[11:00] [11:30] Priya: Pilot idea — small canonical prompt set, measure p95 latency and token cost, and run a small quality eval.
[11:37] Sophie: Sounds great. We'll scope a 2-week pilot.
[11:42] Ethan: For pilot setup, we'll need sample prompts, expected SLOs, and a contact for infra (Marcus).
[11:47] Marcus: I'll provide a Terraform snippet of our current Lambda-NAT setup and a small prompt file.
[11:53] Sophie: Perfect.
[12:00] [12:30] (brief cross talk)
[12:34] Ethan: Sharing the console view of Optimize: suggestions include lowering batch size for low-latency endpoints, enabling KV prefix caching for repeated prompts, and using an 8-bit quantized variant for baseline cost reduction.
[12:50] Marcus: How does KV cache interact with streaming?
[12:53] Ethan: If a prefix is found in cache we can skip full recomputation and start streaming from a cached continuation — effectively reduces token compute. Cache hits show in Console.
[13:08] Priya: Are there compliance constraints around cache TTL?
[13:11] Ethan: TTLs configurable; you can set zero to avoid persistent content, and use compute-only ephemeral caches.
[13:20] [13:30] Janelle: Onboarding timeline — how fast can we go from pilot to production?
[13:34] Sophie: Pilot in 2 weeks, dedicated procurement usually 4–8 weeks after pilot depending on commitments and security review. Private/VPC can add more time for network setup.
[13:48] Priya: Anything else we should consider for chat flow robustness?
[13:52] Ethan: A few practical tips: 1) pre-tokenize to estimate token costs, 2) set conservative max_tokens, 3) use stop sequences for structured replies, 4) implement client-side retries with idempotency keys, 5) monitor fallback events in Console.
[14:12] Sophie: Let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[14:15] Sophie: Action items — Ethan will run perf tests with Atlas sample prompts; Sophie will send pricing and the Dedicated FAQ; Janelle will share SOC2/KMS checklist; Marcus will share infra snippets and prompt set.
[14:30] Priya: We'll also want to see a sample SLA for Dedicated.
[14:35] Sophie: We'll include a short SLA excerpt in the packet.
[14:38] [14:45] (meeting wraps)
[14:48] Ethan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links and the perf schedule.
[14:52] Priya: Thanks, bye.

Post-meeting notes (auto): transcription contains a few mis-hearings (K-V cash -> KV cache, SAMEL -> SAML sometimes), speakers occasionally overlap. Shared assets: deck, security PDF, sample client repo.
